clue.text: Judge more impartial, said the traveller

indicators.note: said tells us the words are to be heard spoken rather than read on the page

parts.note: to judge is to weigh up, and more impartial is fairer: weigh fairer

explanation.surface: A traveller remarks that someone should judge more even-handedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' signals that WEIGH FAIRER, spoken, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A wayfarer is someone journeying on foot, a traveller by road.

clue.text: TV doctor provides answer for reference book

explanation.surface: A television doctor supplies the answer for a reference work.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Who is the TV doctor; asked 'Who?', the answer he provides is Who, so Who is Who; the book lists notable people.
explanation.definitionFit: Who's Who is the annual directory of eminent living people with brief biographies.

clue.text: Peak performances from these singers

parts.note: peak is literal: mountain-top singing, the warbling style of Alpine herdsmen

explanation.surface: These vocalists give their best shows.
explanation.walkthrough: Peak performances sounds like top-form shows, but it means songs from mountain peaks.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpine singers who warble between chest and falsetto voice perform from the mountain tops.

clue.text: He has views of a soulful nature

definitions.text: He has views of a soulful nature

parts.words: He has views of a soulful nature
parts.note: views means beliefs, and nature means the natural world, which such a believer holds to have souls

explanation.surface: A man whose opinions are deeply emotional.
explanation.walkthrough: Soulful nature suggests a sensitive character; read literally, it is the natural world credited with souls.
explanation.definitionFit: Animism is the belief that natural objects such as trees and rivers have spirits.

clue.text: Some held up without equipment for snow?

definitions.text: Some held up without equipment for snow?

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the turned word goes round the snow gear
held up in a down clue means the word is lifted so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a ski is gear for travelling over snow

explanation.surface: Some people were delayed because they lacked snow gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held up' turns the first word over, and 'without' is the old sense of outside. Arctic peoples are certainly not without gear for snow, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Arctic peoples of Greenland, Canada and Alaska were long called by this name, and they live amid snow.

clue.text: Fall follows on this horizontal beam

explanation.surface: Autumn comes after a certain beam laid across a building.
explanation.walkthrough: Fall is the American word for autumn, the season that follows this one; the second sense is the builder's word for a main horizontal timber.
explanation.definitionFit: Autumn comes after the warm season in the year, and in building a summer (as in bressummer) is a large load-bearing horizontal timber.

clue.text: Support for columns in battle, so last of enemy destroyed

indicators.note: destroyed says these letters are broken up and rebuilt in a different arrangement
last of takes only the final letter of the word enemy

explanation.surface: Columns are backed up in a fight, with the final foe wiped out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroyed' rearranges BATTLESO plus Y, the last of enemy. 'Columns' suggests troops, but they are architectural.
explanation.definitionFit: A stylobate is the continuous base or platform on which a row of classical pillars stands.

clue.text: Contents of small pack this prophet has

indicators.note: contents of takes what lies inside each of the three words, losing their outer letters

explanation.surface: A small bag holds something this prophet owns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contents of' takes the middles of small, pack and this: MAL, AC and HI.
explanation.definitionFit: Malachi is the last of the Old Testament minor prophets.

clue.text: Problems done by 5 ac are upsetting scholar

indicators.note: upsetting in a down clue means the run is turned upside down, read bottom to top

parts.note: 5 across is the answer for one who sums, so problems he does are sums

explanation.surface: Some puzzles worked out by someone are troubling a learned man.
explanation.walkthrough: 5 across read as 'one who sums' gives SUMS as his problems; 'upsetting' turns SUMSARE over.
explanation.definitionFit: Erasmus of Rotterdam was the great Renaissance humanist and classical scholar.

clue.text: President opposed to New Deal?

parts.note: the opposite of new is old
deal is a kind of timber, and hickory is another wood, so the question mark allows one wood for another

explanation.surface: A US president who was against Roosevelt's New Deal programme.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to Roosevelt's New Deal, but New and Deal split: deal is pine or fir timber, so another wood stands in for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Hickory was the nickname of Andrew Jackson, seventh President of the United States.

clue.text: Sensibly used to avoid work

explanation.surface: Something employed sensibly so as to dodge labour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Use your loaf' is British slang for 'use your head', so the head is what is sensibly used; the second sense is to idle.
explanation.definitionFit: In rhyming slang loaf (of bread) is the head, the part sensibly used, and to loaf is to lounge about idly.

clue.text: Razor-bill?

parts.note: read as a man called Bill famous for a razor: the medieval philosopher whose principle of economy is known as a razor

explanation.surface: A seabird, the razorbill, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: The razorbill is a seabird, but split it: Bill is a nickname for William, and the friar's principle of cutting away needless assumptions is called his razor.
explanation.definitionFit: William of Occam, the English friar-philosopher, gave his name to Occam's razor, and Bill is short for William.

clue.text: Puts 'ero back in Greek play

indicators.note: back tells us to read the whole of what precedes it from right to left

parts.note: to put something down is to set it, so puts is sets
the clipped Cockney hero, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone hands a hero (dropped aitch) back his part in a Greek drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the whole two-piece run round at once, the dropped aitch of the Cockney hero being kept as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Orestes is a tragedy by Euripides about Agamemnon's son, avenger of his father.

clue.text: Greatness, unfortunately, has alienating effect

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests the letters of the word have met a bad fate and are jumbled

explanation.surface: Being great sadly tends to push people away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges GREATNESS.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange people is to make them hostile or distant, to alienate them.

clue.text: Gets letters in Times, as famous artist

indicators.note: the artist is made by taking the letters found in the words that follow and reordering them

explanation.surface: A celebrated painter gets mentioned in letters to The Times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets letters in' says the answer is made from the letters of TIMES AS, rearranged; the surface suggests letters to the newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Matisse was a leading French painter of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Woman will try to get information from clam, perhaps

parts.note: she refers to a woman
will contracts to 'll
to fish is to probe indirectly for information

explanation.surface: A woman will try to extract details from a tight-lipped person.
explanation.walkthrough: A clam is a byword for a person who says nothing; here it is the mollusc, an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Clams are bivalve molluscs, a type of edible sea creature with a hard covering.

clue.text: Note is placed before the next one in row

parts.note: D is a note of the musical scale
placed means put
the note after D in the scale is E

explanation.surface: A rule of seating: a note is set ahead of the next one in a line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' looks like a line of seats but is a quarrel. The next note after D in the scale is E.
explanation.definitionFit: A row, rhyming with cow, is a noisy quarrel or argument.

clue.text: One member a drunken sot? That's laying it on thick!

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
an MP is a Member of Parliament

indicators.note: drunken suggests the letters are reeling about out of order

explanation.surface: A drunken MP? Somebody is exaggerating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunken' rearranges SOT into STO. 'Laying it on thick' sounds like exaggeration but is applying paint heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: Impasto is the technique of applying paint so heavily that brush or knife marks stand out.

clue.text: Part of Animal Farm — reputation for Orwell, for example

parts.note: a pen is an enclosure for animals on a farm
a person's good name is their reputation

explanation.surface: A section of the novel Animal Farm earned its author his renown.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface names Orwell's novel, but it is just a farm with animals, part of which is an enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell was the assumed literary name of Eric Blair.

clue.text: Main supporters help to deal with pitch

explanation.surface: Key backers help someone cope with a sports field.
explanation.walkthrough: The main is the sea, so its supporters are legs adapted to it; the pitch is a ship's rocking, not a sports ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea legs are the ability to keep balance on a moving ship, which helps a sailor cope with its pitching.

clue.text: Worn by half of Manx race?

definitions.text: Worn by half of Manx race?

parts.words: Worn by half of Manx race?
parts.note: the Isle of Man race is the motorcycle TT, and half of that is one of its two letters; runners in a race also wear this garment

explanation.surface: A garment worn by some of the competitors in a race on the Isle of Man.
explanation.walkthrough: The TT (Tourist Trophy) is the motorcycle race held on the Isle of Man; half of TT is a single T, and athletes wear this sleeveless vest.
explanation.definitionFit: A singlet is a sleeveless vest worn by runners, and one T is half of the Manx TT.

clue.text: Locates sort of plant once used in brewing

indicators.note: sort of signals that the preceding word's letters are sorted into another order

explanation.surface: Someone finds a kind of herb formerly put in beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges LOCATES.
explanation.definitionFit: Alecost, or costmary, is an aromatic herb formerly used to flavour ale.

clue.text: Hold up most of amount to pay out

indicators.note: most of means the word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: a sum is an amount
to spend is to pay money out

explanation.surface: Withhold the bulk of a sum that would be paid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' drops the last letter of SUM to leave SU. 'Hold up' looks like delay, and means hang up.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspend something is to hang it from above, keeping it aloft.

clue.text: Sensation concealed by Chopin, Sand — needlessly

indicators.note: concealed by says the answer lies tucked away within the composer and novelist's names and the adverb

explanation.surface: A feeling hidden by the composer and his lover George Sand, quite unnecessarily.
explanation.walkthrough: Chopin and George Sand were famous lovers, a decoy for the run of letters concealed across the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Pins and needles is the prickling feeling in a limb as numbness wears off.

clue.text: Very big, it was part of a gigantic pile-up

parts.note: OS is the abbreviation for outsize
it in the sense of sex appeal is abbreviated SA

explanation.surface: Something very large was involved in a huge road crash.
explanation.walkthrough: In myth the giants piled Pelion on Ossa to reach heaven; 'pile-up' suggests a motorway crash.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend the giants stacked mountains, Pelion upon this peak in Thessaly, to storm Olympus.

clue.text: With this device, heads off further debate?

definitions.text: With this device, heads off further debate?

parts.words: With this device, heads off further debate?
parts.note: a machine that literally takes heads off, and the parliamentary procedure that cuts debate short by fixed times

explanation.surface: A procedure that forestalls any more argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heads off' reads as forestalls, but it is also literal beheading; in Parliament the name of the device is used for a timetable motion ending debate.
explanation.definitionFit: The French beheading machine also names the parliamentary motion fixing a time to end discussion of a bill.

clue.text: Neat drinks

explanation.surface: Undiluted beverages.
explanation.walkthrough: Neat is an old word for cattle, and cattle are things that low (moo); someone who lowers a pint drinks it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattle make a lowing noise, so they are lowers; and to lower a drink is to swallow it.

clue.text: Treated wound for little boy after sudden pain

indicators.note: after places the boy's name behind the sudden pain in the answer

parts.note: a stitch is a sharp pain in the side
Ed is a short name for a boy called Edward

explanation.surface: A small boy's cut was dressed after he felt a sharp pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Treated wound' reads as a noun phrase, but it is the verb: a wound that has been sewn up.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctors close a cut by sewing it with surgical thread.
